explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Look at how the oath goes: "Surely, as I have planned, so will it be; as I have purposed, so will it stand." (Isaiah 14:24) There's no "might" anywhere in that sentence. When the LORD of Hosts swears, the plan stands.

That's right, friend. The LORD of Hosts says, "Surely, as I have planned, so will it be; as I have purposed, so will it stand." (Isaiah 14:24) He swears it, and nothing in the oath leaves room for the plan to change. I've signed up for plenty of things, and I changed my mind on half of them by lunchtime. That's not how this oath works.
Yes, friend! The LORD says, "I will break Assyria in My land…" (Isaiah 14:25) Straight to the point, no wiggle room. I like a message that doesn't make me squint.

A treaty would mean sitting down and shaking hands, and that's not what's on the table here. The LORD says, "I will break Assyria in My land…" (Isaiah 14:25) That's a plan with a hammer in it, not a pen.

I can see why you'd reach for that one, but it's the opposite direction. The LORD says Assyria is the one who gets broken, and He says it happens in His land. (Isaiah 14:25) No land is being handed out, friend. Assyria is on the receiving end of this plan.
That's it! The LORD says, "I will trample him on My mountain." (Isaiah 14:25) Notice He says "My." It's His land and His mountain, so the plan plays out on His ground.

Close, because deserts make good stories, but the verse doesn't send us there. The LORD says, "I will trample him on My mountain." (Isaiah 14:25) A mountain, friend. Nothing in this verse mentions sand.

You know when a beach day sounds great, but it's not on the schedule? That's this verse. The LORD says, "I will trample him on My mountain." (Isaiah 14:25) So we're looking up at a mountain, not out at the waves.

Right on, friend. The LORD says, "His yoke will be taken off My people, and his burden removed from their shoulders." (Isaiah 14:25) A yoke is a heavy wooden beam that rests on the shoulders, so this is about heavy weight coming off. I think that's the kind of news you'd want to hear twice.
Babylon isn't named in this verse. The LORD says the burden comes off "My people." (Isaiah 14:25) Easy one to mix up, friend, since names start to blur together after a while.

Close, but the verse doesn't point to the soldiers. The LORD says, "His yoke will be taken off My people, and his burden removed from their shoulders." (Isaiah 14:25) The "his" is Assyria, and the relief goes to "My people." That's who gets the weight lifted.
That's it, friend! The message says, "This is the plan devised for the whole earth…" (Isaiah 14:26) The message started with one empire and now it's zoomed all the way out. That's a big plan.
Egypt is a big place, but this verse goes bigger. It says, "This is the plan devised for the whole earth…" (Isaiah 14:26) Egypt is a part of that, friend, not the whole thing.
Moab isn't named in this verse, and the verse is aiming wider than one land. It says, "This is the plan devised for the whole earth…" (Isaiah 14:26) Think bigger, friend. Way bigger.

You've got it, friend. The questions are "…who can thwart Him?" and "…who can turn it back?" (Isaiah 14:27) Nobody steps up, and that's the point. The LORD of Hosts has purposed, and His hand is outstretched.

Good guess, since kings seem to run everything. But the question is "…who can thwart Him?" and nobody stands up to answer it. (Isaiah 14:27) No king is named in this message at all. The only answer left is that no one can.

explanations.answer: Only all the nations together can
explanations.explanation: You'd think a whole crowd could manage it, but the questions hang there with no one answering. "His hand is outstretched, so who can turn it back?" (Isaiah 14:27) Even every nation together doesn't change the answer, friend. The verse before says His hand is "…stretched out over all the nations." (Isaiah 14:26)
